children: Investors sold off U.S. government debt Wednesday, sending Treasury yields to new highs amid mounting concerns about inflation, rising interest rates and the Middle East conflict.
The 10-year benchmark, which has a broad impact on borrowing costs across the economy, rose to 5.07%, the highest since July 2007.

The bonds selloff comes despite efforts by the Treasury Department to cool down long-term yields by increasing its buying of long-term bonds. The department said Wednesday it will buy back as much as $6 billion in 20-year and 30-year bonds on Thursday.
"Markets are sending a message to Secretary [Scott] Bessent that his plan to suppress yields is not likely to work," Spartan Capital's chief market economist Peter Cardillo.
He added that worries about the U.S.'s expanding fiscal deficit are also behind the bonds selloff.
"The bond vigilantes are working at full speed ahead," he said.
The two-year tenor, which is more sensitive to expected Federal Reserve moves, rose to 4.87%, the highest since June 2024, as monetary policymakers indicated that interest rates may go higher.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield reached 5.37%, the highest in 22 years, indicating investors are demanding a higher payout to hold long-term U.S. government debt.

The rise in yields comes amid indications that the U.S. economy is growing fast, which could fuel inflation and drive the Fed to raise rates. September's flash manufacturing PMI was 57, beating a Wall Street Journal consensus forecast of 53.5.
Future markets have now priced in 71% odds of a hike in October, up from 55% Tuesday, according to CME.
Oil prices, another driver of inflation, also advanced Wednesday on rising tensions in the Middle East. Brent was up 3% to $102 a barrel.

title: Ten-Year Treasury Yield Reaches 19-Year High Amid Broad Bonds Selloff
